राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)ले प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन शाहले सरकार सञ्चालनका क्रममा चाल्ने कदममा आफ्नो पूर्ण समर्थन रहने स्पष्ट पारेको छ। पार्टी प्रवक्ता जगदीश खरेलले सरकारका आन्तरिक कामकारबाहीमा पार्टीले हस्तक्षेप नगर्ने बताएका छन्।

विमानस्थलमा सांसदहरूको बिदाइका क्रममा सञ्चारकर्मीसँग कुरा गर्दै खरेलले सरकारलाई स्वतन्त्र रूपमा काम गर्ने वातावरण दिनुपर्ने पार्टीको धारणा रहेको बताए।

सरकारअन्तर्गतका निकाय तथा व्यक्तिहरूका विषयमा पार्टीले अत्यधिक चासो राख्दा हस्तक्षेप गरेको अर्थ लाग्न सक्ने उनको भनाइ छ। त्यसैले यस्ता विषयमा निर्णय गर्ने जिम्मेवारी प्रधानमन्त्रीकै भएको उनले स्पष्ट पारे।

‘प्रधानमन्त्रीज्यूले केही कुरा गलत भइरहेको छ र अब एक्सन लिनुपर्छ भन्ने महसुस गर्नुभयो भने उहाँले चाल्ने कदममा पार्टीको सम्पूर्ण समर्थन रहन्छ,’ खरेलले भने।

गृहमन्त्री, प्रधानमन्त्रीका सल्लाहकार तथा सरकारका अन्य व्यक्तिहरूका विषयमा सार्वजनिक रूपमा उठिरहेका प्रश्नहरू पार्टीको औपचारिक छलफलमा प्रवेश नगरेको पनि उनले जानकारी दिए। ती विषयमा प्रधानमन्त्रीको धारणा र सरकारले गरिरहेको कामबारे पार्टीले प्रतीक्षा गरिरहेको उनको भनाइ छ।

पार्टी सभापति, महामन्त्रीसहित सम्पूर्ण नेतृत्व सरकार सञ्चालनमा कुनै अवरोध वा हस्तक्षेपको महसुस नहोस् भन्नेमा सचेत रहेको पनि खरेलले बताए।

त्यस्तै, नेपाल प्रहरीका महानिरीक्षक (आईजीपी) लाई हटाउने वा निरन्तरता दिने विषयमा पार्टीले सरकारलाई कुनै निर्देशन नदिएको उनले स्पष्ट पारे। यो सरकारको विवेक र निर्णयमा निर्भर रहने विषय भएको उनको भनाइ छ।

उक्त विषय अदालतसम्म पुगेको र केही प्रक्रिया अघि बढिरहेको अवस्थामा सरकारले आवश्यकताअनुसार थप स्पष्ट पार्दै जाने उनले बताए।

Bodybuilder Eddie Abbew Calls Whey Protein a ‘Scam’: ‘Just Eat an Egg’
The former professional bodybuilder questions the supplement industry's marketing claims, citing personal digestive problems and advocating whole-food protein sources.

Former professional bodybuilder Eddie Abbew has criticised the widespread use of whey protein supplements, arguing that people should prioritise whole foods such as eggs to meet their daily protein requirements.

In a video titled The Real Reason Why I Stopped Drinking Whey Protein!, shared on YouTube, Abbew outlined five reasons behind his decision to stop consuming the popular bodybuilding supplement.

Known for his outspoken views on fitness and nutrition, Abbew questioned the supplement industry's influence on bodybuilding culture and challenged the idea that protein powders are essential for building muscle.

"If you want protein, eat a f***ing egg," he said in the video.
Five reasons behind his decision
Abbew explained that his first concern involved the origins and processing of whey protein. He claimed that whey was historically treated as a dairy by-product and that its transformation into a widely marketed fitness supplement was driven partly by commercial interests.

He also recalled how bodybuilding magazines and prominent athletes helped popularise whey protein during the 1990s, making it a staple among fitness enthusiasts.

His second and third concerns were related to his personal health experiences.

Abbew said he had experienced persistent testicular discomfort and digestive problems, including diarrhoea, while consuming whey protein. He recalled removing the supplement from his diet after receiving a social media comment questioning its possible effects on prostate health.

According to Abbew, his discomfort improved after he stopped consuming whey protein.

He also described experiencing frequent bloating after drinking protein shakes, which he partly associated with his lactose intolerance.

However, these are his personal experiences and do not independently establish that whey protein caused his symptoms.
Questions over ingredients and marketing
The fourth reason involved the ingredients used in commercial protein powders.

Abbew criticised products containing multiple additives, flavourings, thickeners and other processed ingredients. During the video, he read out the ingredient list of a whey protein product and argued that consumers should pay closer attention to what they are purchasing.

He described the product as more of a science experiment than food and questioned why people rely so heavily on processed supplements when protein is available through everyday foods.

His fifth concern focused on scientific research and the marketing of whey protein.

Abbew questioned whether some studies promoting whey protein were influenced by companies with commercial interests in the supplement industry. He also challenged claims about its bioavailability and absorption.

He argued that people should consider the broader nutritional value of their diets rather than focusing exclusively on protein intake.
Whole foods versus protein supplements
Throughout the video, Abbew encouraged viewers to obtain protein from whole-food sources, including eggs, meat, fish and chicken.

He argued that bodybuilding nutrition should not depend excessively on commercially marketed supplements.

However, whey protein is a dairy-derived protein that provides essential amino acids and can be a convenient way to increase protein intake. Its nutritional value and suitability depend on the individual, product formulation and dietary needs.

People with lactose intolerance may also experience digestive discomfort from certain whey products, although lactose-free alternatives are available.

Abbew's comments have brought renewed attention to the debate over protein supplements and the role of whole foods in bodybuilding.

While his personal experiences explain why he stopped consuming whey protein, his broader claims about its safety and nutritional value should not be treated as established scientific conclusions.

India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has defended the government's authority over visa decisions, describing them as sovereign functions, following reports that Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng and several other foreign invitees faced visa denials or cancellations ahead of the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad.

Speaking at his regular media briefing on Friday, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said visa decisions fall within the sovereign authority of individual governments.

"Visa matters are sovereign functions of any country or any government. So that is what I have to say," Jaiswal stated.

His remarks came amid reports that more than 100 foreign invitees to the Bharat Summit had their visas denied or revoked, while over 300 others reportedly received clearance to attend the event.

Norwegian Journalist Says Visa Was Cancelled Before Departure
Helle Lyng, an independent journalist based in Norway, claimed that her Indian visa was cancelled shortly before she was due to leave for Hyderabad.

Lyng had been invited as a panelist and speaker at the Bharat Summit, where she was scheduled to participate in a discussion on the future of media and press freedom.

In a post on X, she questioned the decision, saying she had already received a visa from the Indian Embassy in Norway and was preparing to travel when it was revoked.

She alleged that the cancellation came on the instructions of higher authorities in India's Ministry of Home Affairs.

Lyng had previously attracted attention during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Oslo in May, when she raised a question concerning press freedom with the Indian side.

Congress Criticises Government Over Visa Cancellation
The Congress party strongly criticised the reported cancellation of Lyng's visa, questioning the government's response to journalists raising difficult questions.

In a post on X, the opposition party referred to Lyng's earlier interaction with Modi and questioned why she was prevented from attending the Hyderabad summit.

The party also raised concerns over the government's approach towards questions about press freedom and accountability.

Bharat Summit Held in Hyderabad
The Bharat Summit, organised by the Congress, is being held in Hyderabad on November 13 and 14.

Lyng was among the invited international participants expected to contribute to discussions on media, journalism and press freedom.

The reported visa cancellations have drawn attention to the participation of foreign speakers at the event, although the MEA has maintained that visa decisions remain within the sovereign authority of governments.

राष्ट्रपति मुइज्जुले उक्त निर्णय प्यालेस्टाइनप्रतिको आफ्नो सरकार र जनताको समर्थनसँग सम्बन्धित रहेको बताएका छन्। उनले प्यालेस्टिनीमाथि इजरायलले गरेको कारबाहीलाई नरसंहारको संज्ञा दिँदै इजरायली पासपोर्टधारीलाई प्रवेश अनुमति दिनु सरकारको अडानविपरीत हुने बताएका छन्।

माल्दिभ्सले अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मञ्चहरूमा प्यालेस्टिनी अधिकारको समर्थन गर्दै आएको छ। उसले पूर्वी जेरुसेलमलाई राजधानी बनाएर सन् १९६७ अघिका सीमामा आधारित स्वतन्त्र प्यालेस्टिनी राष्ट्रको पक्षमा आवाज उठाउँदै आएको छ।

🛂 दोहोरो नागरिकता भएकालाई के हुन्छ?
प्रस्तावित प्रतिबन्धले अर्को देशको पासपोर्टसमेत भएका इजरायली नागरिकको प्रवेशबारे प्रश्न उठाएको छ। हालको व्यवस्था मुख्यतः इजरायली पासपोर्टधारीमा केन्द्रित रहेकाले दोहोरो नागरिकता भएका व्यक्तिले अर्को देशको पासपोर्ट प्रयोग गरेर प्रवेश गर्न सक्ने सम्भावना रहन्छ।

राष्ट्रपति मुइज्जुले यो सीमिततालाई स्वीकार गर्दै इजरायली नागरिक तथा इजरायलसँग सम्बन्धित संस्थाहरूको घरजग्गा लगानीमा समेत प्रतिबन्ध लगाउने छुट्टै कानुनी प्रस्ताव रहेको बताएका छन्। उक्त व्यवस्था लागू भए पासपोर्ट जुनसुकै देशको भए पनि निश्चित विकास परियोजनामा लगानी गर्न रोक लाग्न सक्नेछ।

🏝️ पर्यटन गन्तव्यमा नयाँ अध्यागमन नीति
विश्वभरका पर्यटकमाझ विलासी रिसोर्ट, सेता समुद्री किनार र नीलो पानीका लागि चर्चित माल्दिभ्सले सन् २०२५ अप्रिलमा अध्यागमन ऐन संशोधन गर्दै इजरायली पासपोर्टधारीलाई प्रवेशमा रोक लगाएको थियो।

इजरायलले पनि आफ्ना नागरिकलाई माल्दिभ्स भ्रमण नगर्न सुझाव दिँदै आएको थियो। त्यहाँ इजरायलविरोधी भावना र आपत्कालीन अवस्थामा सहयोग प्राप्त गर्न कठिनाइ हुन सक्ने उसको चिन्ता थियो।

राष्ट्रपति मुइज्जुले अघि सारेको नयाँ संशोधन संसद्बाट छलफल र अनुमोदन भएपछि मात्र लागू हुनेछ। त्यसअघि भने हालको अध्यागमन प्रतिबन्ध नै कायम रहनेछ।

विराटनगर किंग्सका कप्तान सन्दीप लामिछानेले व्यक्तिगत कीर्तिमानभन्दा टोलीको जित आफ्नो मुख्य प्राथमिकता रहेको बताएका छन्। नेपाल प्रिमियर लिग (एनपिएल) अन्तर्गत बिहीबार पोखरा एभेन्जर्सविरुद्ध ह्याट्रिकसहित ६ विकेट लिएर टोलीलाई जित दिलाएपछि उनले यस्तो प्रतिक्रिया दिएका हुन्।

सन्दीपले ४ ओभरमा २७ रन खर्चेर ६ विकेट लिए। यो उनको एनपिएल करिअरकै उत्कृष्ट बलिङ प्रदर्शन हो। उनको घातक बलिङका कारण पोखरा एभेन्जर्सले दिएको १३३ रनको लक्ष्य पछ्याएको विराटनगरले ४ विकेटको जित निकाल्यो।

🏏 संकटमा इसुरु र शेहानको साथ

लक्ष्य पछ्याउने क्रममा विराटनगरले ७८ रनमै पाँच विकेट गुमाएपछि खेल कठिन बनेको थियो। तर इसुरु उदाना र शेहान जयसूर्याले अविजित ३१ रनको साझेदारी गर्दै टोलीलाई जितसम्म पुर्‍याए।

आन्द्रे रसेलको स्थानमा टोलीमा आएका इसुरुको प्रदर्शनबाट सन्दीप प्रभावित देखिए। उनले दबाबपूर्ण परिस्थितिमा आफूलाई ढाल्न सक्ने इसुरुको क्षमताको प्रशंसा गरे। बासिर अहमद र शेहान जयसूर्याको योगदानलाई पनि उनले महत्वपूर्ण बताए।

🏆 व्यक्तिगत उपलब्धिभन्दा जित महत्वपूर्ण

ह्याट्रिकसहित ६ विकेट लिए पनि सन्दीपले व्यक्तिगत उपलब्धिभन्दा टोलीको सफलतालाई ठूलो माने। आफूले एक विकेट लिए पनि पाँच विकेट लिए पनि टोलीले जित्दा उत्तिकै खुसी हुने उनको भनाइ थियो।

उनले आफ्नो बलिङ क्षमताप्रति विश्वास व्यक्त गर्दै नतिजा जे भए पनि टोलीका लागि योगदान गर्ने लक्ष्य रहने बताए।

📊 प्लेअफ सम्भावना बलियो, अब अन्तिम खेलमा ध्यान

पोखराविरुद्धको जितसँगै विराटनगर अंक तालिकाको शीर्ष चारमा उक्लिएको छ। यसले टोलीको प्लेअफ सम्भावना बलियो बनाएको छ।

सन्दीपका अनुसार टोलीको प्राथमिकता नेट रनरेट सुधार्नुभन्दा खेल जितेर दुई अंक जोड्नु थियो। अब विराटनगरले आफ्नो अन्तिम लिग खेलमा कोलम्बो लायन्सविरुद्ध राम्रो प्रदर्शन गर्ने लक्ष्य राखेको छ।

उनले प्रतियोगिताभर बलिङ युनिटले गरेको सामूहिक प्रयासको प्रशंसा गर्दै नेपाली क्रिकेटको विकासका लागि अनुभवी खेलाडीहरूको साथ र उपस्थिति महत्वपूर्ण हुने पनि बताएका छन्।

मकवानपुरको भीमफेदी गाउँपालिका–६ स्थित चिसापानीगढीमा भएको यात्रुवाहक विद्युतीय गाडी (ईभी) दुर्घटनाको कारण पत्ता लगाउन पाँच सदस्यीय छानबिन समिति गठन गरिएको छ। बिहीबार बिहान भएको दुर्घटनामा १४ जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ भने छ जना घाइते भएका छन्।

मकवानपुरका प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी वसन्त अधिकारीका अनुसार सहायक प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी शेषकान्त पौडेलको संयोजकत्वमा समिति गठन गरिएको हो। समितिलाई दुर्घटनाको कारण पहिचान गरी एक साताभित्र प्रतिवेदन बुझाउने जिम्मेवारी दिइएको छ।

समितिमा जिल्ला ट्राफिक प्रहरी कार्यालय मकवानपुरका प्रहरी निरीक्षक रमेश विष्ट, प्रहरी निरीक्षक उमाशंकर प्रसाद, प्रदेशको पूर्वाधार विकास कार्यालयका एक इन्जिनियर र बागमती प्रदेशको आन्तरिक मामिला तथा कानुन मन्त्रालयका कानुन अधिकृत सदस्य छन्।

समितिले दुर्घटनाका बेला सवारीसाधनको क्षमताभन्दा बढी यात्रु राखिएको थियो कि थिएन, रुट इजाजतको अवस्था, चालकको अवस्था तथा सडकको भौतिक अवस्थाबारे अनुसन्धान गर्नेछ। साथै, आगामी दिनमा यस्ता दुर्घटना न्यूनीकरण गर्न अपनाउनुपर्ने उपायसमेत प्रतिवेदनमा समेटिनेछ।

प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी अधिकारीका अनुसार भीमफेदी–देउराली सडकखण्डमा पछिल्लो १३ महिनामा तीनवटा ठूला दुर्घटना भइसकेका छन्। उनले सवारीसाधनमा लागू गरिएको ‘टाइम कार्ड’ मात्रै दुर्घटना रोक्न पर्याप्त नभएको भन्दै सडक सुरक्षामा तत्काल सुधार आवश्यक रहेको बताएका छन्।

बिहीबार बिहान काठमाडौंबाट सर्लाहीतर्फ जाँदै गरेको मधेश प्रदेश ०३–००१ ज ०८८० नम्बरको ईभी सडकबाट करिब ५०० मिटर तल खसेर दुर्घटनाग्रस्त भएको थियो।

नर्वेली पत्रकार हेल्ले लिङको भारत भ्रमण उडानको केही घण्टाअघि नै रोकिएको छ। भारतको हैदराबादमा नोभेम्बर १२ देखि १४ सम्म आयोजना हुने ‘भारत समिट’ मा सहभागी हुन जान लागेकी उनको भिसा भारतीय दूतावासले अन्तिम समयमा रद्द गरेको हो।

लिङ ओस्लोबाट बुधबार हैदराबाद जाने तयारीमा थिइन्। उनी तेलंगाना सरकारद्वारा आयोजित उक्त सम्मेलनमा ‘द फ्युचर अफ मिडिया’ अर्थात् सञ्चारमाध्यमको भविष्य विषयक छलफलमा सहभागी हुने कार्यक्रम थियो। सम्मेलन अवधिका लागि उनलाई एकपटक प्रवेश गर्न मिल्ने वैध भिसासमेत जारी गरिएको थियो।

तर विमानस्थल जानुअघि नै नर्वेस्थित भारतीय दूतावासबाट फोन आएर उनको भिसा रद्द गरिएको र भारत यात्रा गर्न नपाउने जानकारी दिइएको उनले बताएकी छन्। उनलाई भिसा औपचारिक रूपमा रद्द गर्न दूतावासमै उपस्थित हुनसमेत भनिएको थियो।

‘यो स्तब्ध पार्ने र अचम्मलाग्दो छ,’ लिङले *द वायर*सँग कुरा गर्दै भनेकी छन्। राजनीतिक अनुमति पाएपछि नै भिसा जारी भएको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले भारतको गृह मन्त्रालयले आफूलाई प्रवेश अनुमति नदिने निर्णय गर्नुको कारण बुझ्न नसकेको बताएकी छन्।

भिसा रद्द गर्नुको आधिकारिक कारण भने उपलब्ध विवरणमा खुलाइएको छैन।

A NEW LIFE ENTERS THE OCEAN, SURROUNDED BY FAMILY.

On November 2, 2025, whale-watching boats off Skjervøy, northern Norway, witnessed an extraordinary event: an orca giving birth in the wild.

Footage captured the mother surrounded by other members of her pod as the newborn entered the water. The sighting offered a rare glimpse into a moment that scientists have seldom documented in the open ocean.

The newborn's first moments are critical. It must reach the surface to breathe, while its family stays close during this vulnerable beginning.

Source: Live Science, November 7, 2025.

CAN WILD ANIMALS REMEMBER AN ACT OF KINDNESS?

A story shared by fishermen tells of a man who freed a young dolphin trapped near his dock. Later, a dolphin reportedly began returning to the same spot, lifting fish toward the wooden planks as if offering gifts.

The story is touching, but there is no verified evidence proving the dolphin was the same animal or that the fish were expressions of gratitude. Still, dolphins are highly intelligent animals capable of learning, remembering individuals and forming strong social bonds.

Perhaps we cannot know what the dolphin intended, but the story raises a beautiful question: can animals remember the kindness humans show them?

ONE OF THE ATLANTIC'S BIGGEST KNOWN MALE GREAT WHITE SHARKS IS ON THE MOVE.

Contender, the largest male white shark ever tagged by OCEARCH in the Western North Atlantic, has been detected approximately nine miles south of Atlantic City, New Jersey.

After spending around four months in Atlantic Canada, the giant shark is heading south as part of its seasonal migration toward warmer waters.

His movements are being monitored through satellite tracking, giving researchers valuable insight into the migration patterns of great white sharks and helping improve our understanding of these important ocean predators.

Source: OCEARCH.

GIANTS OF THE OCEAN MAKE AN UNEXPECTED VISIT TO NEW YORK CITY.

Boaters and onlookers captured remarkable close-up footage of humpback whales surfacing in New York Harbor and the Hudson River on Wednesday and Thursday.

Seeing these enormous marine mammals so close to one of the world's busiest cities is an extraordinary sight. Their presence also highlights the importance of protecting urban waterways that whales and other marine animals continue to visit.

After four months of treatment and rehabilitation, Anmoki has finally returned to the ocean.

The young Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin was rescued from Gangneung Port, South Korea, on July 15 after suffering serious injuries, including a deep wound caused by repeated encounters with boat propellers.

Veterinarians and marine specialists helped Anmoki recover. Officials confirmed that the dolphin regained normal swimming abilities and could hunt live fish again.

On November 12, 2026, Anmoki was released near Jeju Island, returning to the wild with a satellite tracker to monitor the journey ahead.

A second chance at freedom. May the ocean welcome Anmoki home.

Source: SBS News, November 12, 2026.

A young fin whale washed into the surf at Cowell Beach in Santa Cruz, California, on November 12, 2026. Despite the response from marine mammal experts, the whale died at approximately 10 a.m.

Experts reported that the whale was severely underweight and showed signs of long-term illness. Its exact cause of death remains unknown, and a necropsy is planned to investigate what happened.

The beach was closed while responders worked to remove the enormous animal and protect public safety.

A heartbreaking reminder that even the ocean's giants can become vulnerable.

Sources: NBC Bay Area; UC Santa Cruz Long Marine Laboratory; The Marine Mammal Center.

A group of seven orcas targeted a lone humpback whale in a dramatic encounter. But the larger whale did not give up without a fight.

The humpback rolled onto its back, using its powerful body and enormous pectoral fins to defend itself against the attackers.

Humpback whales are known to confront orcas, sometimes even putting themselves at risk to protect other animals. Encounters like this reveal how unpredictable life in the ocean can be.

They were moved from a closed marine park in Canada in an effort to give them another chance. But the relocation of 30 beluga whales from Marineland has been followed by six deaths.

One of them was Peekachu, a 23-year-old female who died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium just days after arriving. Caretakers had raised concerns about dehydration, while later examinations identified serious pre-existing health problems.

Other belugas also died at facilities in Chicago, Spain, and San Diego. A dolphin named Echo, also transferred from Marineland, died in Spain.

The deaths have raised difficult questions about the animals’ years in captivity, their health before transport, and whether moving them to other aquariums was the best available option.

Rescue should mean more than moving animals from one tank to another.

Sources: Mongabay, October 21, 2026; Associated Press; Whale Sanctuary Project.

America's newest stealth bomber just hit a major milestone.

For the first time, the B-21 Raider has released conventional weapons in flight, in a test last week at Edwards Air Force Base.

The fascinating part is how they got there. Before the real release, engineers ran thousands of hours of modeling inside the B-21's "digital twin", a detailed virtual copy of the aircraft, to predict and perfect the weapon's trajectory before a single real one ever left the jet. The Air Force says it speeds up adding new weapons and cuts repeated physical testing.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach: "We are building an impressive fleet that will give our joint force credible, penetrating strike options for decades to come."

The Raider is set to begin arriving at Ellsworth Air Force Base in 2027.

US soldiers in China during a ceremony to receive the remains of a fallen airman who went missing in World War II. A Chinese honor guard transfers the recently discovered remains of the US airman. He is believed to have gone missing while flying over "the Hump" as part of the airlift to resupply China.

The US Air Force just rewrote its plan for the future, and it's less about new jets than about sensors, networks and AI.

It's called Force Design 2026, and the Air Force's Chief of Staff, Gen. Ken Wilsbach, calls it "a fundamental shift" in how the service approaches air defense.

The big idea: move away from chasing down and destroying threats one at a time, and toward seeing, networking and deciding faster, with autonomy and AI working alongside aircraft. The focus is on "denied environments", where an enemy is trying to jam or blind US forces.

Outnumbered and taking fire from three sides, the four SEALs fought through a relentless, three-hour running gun battle. Every man was hit multiple times.

Trapped down in a ravine, the steep granite cliffs blocked all radio and satellite signals. Murphy knew with absolute certainty: without emergency close air support, none of his men were walking off that mountain alive.

Knowing it was almost certain death, Lieutenant Murphy made a leader's choice.

He deliberately walked out of cover onto an exposed, open rock ledge directly in the line of sight of dozens of enemy machine guns to get a satellite signal.

Calm under fire, Murphy dialed headquarters and relayed their exact coordinates: "My men are taking heavy fire... we're getting picked apart."

As he spoke, an enemy bullet punched through his back. He dropped the phone, picked it back up, finished the transmission, and signed off with words that will live forever in military history:

"Thank you, sir."

Mortally wounded, Murphy crawled back to his fighting position and continued returning fire alongside his men until his last breath.

His final transmission allowed the rescue force to scramble, ultimately saving the life of Marcus Luttrell.

In 2007, Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first service member to receive the nation’s highest award for valor in the War in Afghanistan.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

He refused to carry a weapon into battle. His own side called him a coward for it.

Desmond Doss was a Seventh-day Adventist who believed he could serve his country without taking a life. The Army mocked him and tried to push him out, then trained him as a combat medic and sent him to the Pacific.

On Okinawa, in the spring of 1945, his unit had to climb a cliff some 400 feet high that the men called Hacksaw Ridge. When a Japanese counterattack forced the Americans back, dozens of wounded were left stranded at the top. Doss refused to leave.

Alone and under fire, he went back again and again, lowering wounded men down the cliff face one at a time with a rope sling. Each time, he prayed the same thing: "Lord, please help me get one more." He kept going for hours. The Army credits him with saving about 75 men that day.

Days later he was wounded by a grenade, rolled off his own rescue litter to treat another man, and was then hit by a sniper. He splinted his shattered arm with a rifle stock and crawled to safety.

In 1945, he became the first conscientious objector in American history to receive the Medal of Honor. He never fired a shot at the enemy, and he saved more lives in one day than most men save in a lifetime.

Aaron Kenefick, Gunnery Sgt. Edwin Johnson, and Hospital Corpsman 3rd Class James Layton.

The Marines rejected him. So did the Navy and the paratroopers. He was too small and too young-looking, barely 5'5" and slight.

Three years later, Audie Murphy was the most decorated American soldier of World War II.

Born into a poor Texas sharecropping family, one of twelve children, he left school around the fifth grade to pick cotton. He finally got into the Army in 1942 and fought across Sicily, Italy, Anzio, France, and Germany with the 3rd Infantry Division.

On January 26, 1945, near Holtzwihr, France, his depleted company was attacked by German infantry and tanks. Murphy ordered his men back, then climbed onto a burning tank destroyer and used its machine gun to hold off the enemy almost single-handedly for nearly an hour, wounded, directing artillery by phone. For that, he earned the Medal of Honor.

He went on to Hollywood, made more than 40 films, and played himself in "To Hell and Back." He also spoke openly about the nightmares war left him, long before anyone called it PTSD.

He died in 1971 and rests at Arlington, his grave one of the most visited in America.

He was already on fire… and he still went back in.

A Swedish soldier with the Automatkarbin 5, better known as the Ak 5. For close to four decades, this rifle has been the face of the Swedish Armed Forces. But early problems with the new rifle meant the Ak 5 had to step back up as a primary rifle once again. Retirement will have to wait a little longer.

June 28, 2005. The Hindu Kush mountains of Kunar Province, Afghanistan.

Deep behind enemy lines during Operation Red Wings, a 4-man Navy SEAL reconnaissance team—commanded by 29-year-old Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy—was ambushed on a sheer mountain ridgeline by over 50 Taliban fighters.

Outnumbered and taking fire from three sides, the four SEALs fought through a relentless, three-hour running gun battle. Every man was hit multiple times.

Trapped down in a ravine, the steep granite cliffs blocked all radio and satellite signals. Murphy knew with absolute certainty: without emergency close air support, none of his men were walking off that mountain alive.

Knowing it was almost certain death, Lieutenant Murphy made a leader's choice.

He deliberately walked out of cover onto an exposed, open rock ledge directly in the line of sight of dozens of enemy machine guns to get a satellite signal.

Calm under fire, Murphy dialed headquarters and relayed their exact coordinates: "My men are taking heavy fire... we're getting picked apart."

As he spoke, an enemy bullet punched through his back. He dropped the phone, picked it back up, finished the transmission, and signed off with words that will live forever in military history:

"Thank you, sir."

Mortally wounded, Murphy crawled back to his fighting position and continued returning fire alongside his men until his last breath.

His final transmission allowed the rescue force to scramble, ultimately saving the life of Marcus Luttrell.

In 2007, Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first service member to receive the nation’s highest award for valor in the War in Afghanistan.

A leader never asks his men to do what he isn't willing to do himself.

“SHOULD TAXPAYER WELFARE CASH BE RESTRICTED TO BASIC SURVIVAL NEEDS?” — Florida has become the first state in the country to implement strict new regulations blocking public assistance cash benefits from being spent on tattoos, vaping products, theme park admissions, and other luxury services as part of a statewide crackdown on welfare fraud and waste.

“We think that will ultimately save taxpayer money and reduce fraud, but also will help our efforts to get folks the true help that they need. At its core, this is about responsible stewardship and making sure taxpayer resources support family stability and self-sufficiency, not luxury purchases.”

— Florida Governor Ron DeSantis

Key Elements of Florida's Welfare Reform
First-in-the-Nation TANF Amendment: Florida officially amended its Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) State Plan to establish explicit point-of-sale and ATM withdrawal bans for non-essential purchases on state-issued Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards.

Prohibited Business & Service Categories: The updated restrictions bar cash-assistance benefits from being spent at tattoo and piercing studios, vape and tobacco shops, theme parks and entertainment attractions, casinos and gaming parlors, tanning salons, adult entertainment venues, and luxury spas.

Focusing on Essential Family Needs: Administered through the Florida Department of Children and Families, the measure mandates that cash welfare benefits be directed exclusively toward essential living costs—including food, housing, utilities, child clothing, and job-training expenses.

Potential National Blueprint: The policy establishes a precedent currently being evaluated by federal lawmakers and multiple other state legislatures seeking to tighten public assistance spending rules nationwide.

The Public Debate
Arguments in Favor: Supporters emphasize that public assistance programs exist as temporary safety nets funded by hardworking taxpayers. Restricting non-essential spending protects program integrity, deters benefit trafficking, and ensures public funds directly aid struggling children and families.

Arguments in Opposition: Critics contend that TANF cash stipends are already very limited (averaging around $300 per month for a family of three in Florida) with strict work requirements, arguing that new merchant-category prohibitions create additional administrative friction and unfairly stigmatize assistance recipients.

Paratroopers don't clock out. When gunfire erupted outside his apartment building, Sergeant Brian Lieberman didn't lock his door and wait for the police. On June 5, 2023, then-Specialist Brian R. Lieberman—a combat medic with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division—was off-duty at his apartment complex in Fayetteville, North Carolina, when rapid gunfire shattered the evening quiet.

Without body armor or advanced medical equipment, he grabbed his legally owned firearm and sprinted downstairs toward the active shooter:

Sprinting to the Fire: Arriving in the courtyard, Lieberman identified himself as an Army combat medic and located a female victim suffering from a critical penetrating sucking chest wound.

Shielding Under Secondary Fire: As he began treating her, the active shooter circled back in a vehicle and opened fire directly at them. Lieberman threw his body across the wounded woman to act as a human shield, drew his sidearm, returned fire, and drove the shooter away.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

“Without a doubt our Airborne medics move to the sound of gunfire to save lives,” said Col. Schuerger. “Of course he moved to the sound of gunfire, of course he administered aid, of course he saved somebody's life.”

Lieberman’s guidance to fellow medics reflects the heart of the Airborne:

“I always tell my junior medics to never lose their passion for the craft of medicine. That way no matter where they are, no matter what they're doing, they can always be there for someone on their worst day.”

All American valor in action.

June 12, 2011 -- For two Marines attached to Marine Embedded Training Team 2-8, Regional Corps Advisory Command 3-7, in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, the morning of Sept. 8, 2009 started simple enough.

Then the world exploded around them.

Their actions during the ensuing fight earned them the nation’s second-highest award for valor. Secretary of the Navy Ray Mabus presented Capt. Ademola D. Fabayo and Staff Sgt. Juan J. Rodriguez-Chavez with the Navy Cross during a ceremony at the National Museum of the Marine Corps on June 10.

On that fateful day, then 1st Lt. Fabayo was leading a dismounted patrol of Americans and two platoons of Afghan National Security Forces into Ganjgal Village for a pre-dawn meeting with village elders. A short distance away, Rodriguez-Chavez was part of the team’s security element, ready to help his teammates if necessary.

The team was attacked by more than 50 enemy fighters, who rained down machine gun fire and rocket-propelled grenades from fortified positions. Four members of the team were cut off and exposed to the murderous fire.

With no regard for his own life, Fabayo pushed forward on foot into the kill zone in an attempt to regain contact, effectively engaging the enemy at close range with his M4 rifle. When a U.S. Army advisor was severely wounded, Fabayo moved from a covered position under heavy fire to assist in his recovery, helping carry him across several hundred meters of fire-swept ground.

He then gotten into an unarmored truck with another advisor and pushed back into the kill zone, ignoring the rounds striking the truck, as they attempted to rescue the fallen members of their team.

While Fabayo was attacking, Rodriguez-Chavez wasted no time getting into the fight as well. With members of his team in immediate danger, he drove a gun truck, with one other Marine as his gunner, forward into the kill zone of the ambush with only the machine gun fire of his gunner to suppress the enemy. He repeatedly ignored the heavy enemy fire and drove the vehicle into the kill zone three times to cover the withdrawal of the force and evacuate two dozen members of the Afghan National Security Forces.

The two Marines, along with two other members of their team, then consolidated their force into an armored Humvee, Rodriguez-Chavez at the wheel and Fabayo in the gunners turret, manning the machine gun. They made yet another extremely hazardous trip into the deepest point of the kill zone, where Rodriguez-Chavez positioned his vehicle to shield his teammates from the intense enemy fire as they dismounted to recover the fallen warriors.

During the ceremony, Mabus said that the Marines repeatedly exposed themselves to enemy fire and demonstrated the kind of valor that should be taught to every Marine in boot camp.

Mortally wounded, Murphy crawled back to his fighting position and continued returning fire alongside his men until his last breath.

His final transmission allowed the rescue force to scramble, ultimately saving the life of Marcus Luttrell.

Key Elements of Florida's Welfare Reform
First-in-the-Nation TANF Amendment: Florida officially amended its Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) State Plan to establish explicit point-of-sale and ATM withdrawal bans for non-essential purchases on state-issued Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards.

Prohibited Business & Service Categories: The updated restrictions bar cash-assistance benefits from being spent at tattoo and piercing studios, vape and tobacco shops, theme parks and entertainment attractions, casinos and gaming parlors, tanning salons, adult entertainment venues, and luxury spas.

Focusing on Essential Family Needs: Administered through the Florida Department of Children and Families, the measure mandates that cash welfare benefits be directed exclusively toward essential living costs—including food, housing, utilities, child clothing, and job-training expenses.

Potential National Blueprint: The policy establishes a precedent currently being evaluated by federal lawmakers and multiple other state legislatures seeking to tighten public assistance spending rules nationwide.

The Public Debate
Arguments in Favor: Supporters emphasize that public assistance programs exist as temporary safety nets funded by hardworking taxpayers. Restricting non-essential spending protects program integrity, deters benefit trafficking, and ensures public funds directly aid struggling children and families.

Arguments in Opposition: Critics contend that TANF cash stipends are already very limited (averaging around $300 per month for a family of three in Florida) with strict work requirements, arguing that new merchant-category prohibitions create additional administrative friction and unfairly stigmatize assistance recipients.

“PARATROOPERS DON’T CLOCK OUT: HEARD GUNSHOTS & RAN DOWNSTAIRS WITH IMPROVISED MEDICAL GEAR.”

Paratroopers don't clock out. When gunfire erupted outside his apartment building, Sergeant Brian Lieberman didn't lock his door and wait for the police. He ran straight into the courtyard, found a victim with an open chest wound, and built an airtight chest seal with plastic wrap and tape to keep her lungs from collapsing.

On June 5, 2023, then-Specialist Brian R. Lieberman—a combat medic with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division—was off-duty at his apartment complex in Fayetteville, North Carolina, when rapid gunfire shattered the evening quiet.

Without body armor or advanced medical equipment, he grabbed his legally owned firearm and sprinted downstairs toward the active shooter:

Sprinting to the Fire: Arriving in the courtyard, Lieberman identified himself as an Army combat medic and located a female victim suffering from a critical penetrating sucking chest wound.

Shielding Under Secondary Fire: As he began treating her, the active shooter circled back in a vehicle and opened fire directly at them. Lieberman threw his body across the wounded woman to act as a human shield, drew his sidearm, returned fire, and drove the shooter away.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

“Without a doubt our Airborne medics move to the sound of gunfire to save lives,” said Col. Schuerger. “Of course he moved to the sound of gunfire, of course he administered aid, of course he saved somebody's life.”

Lieberman’s guidance to fellow medics reflects the heart of the Airborne:

“I always tell my junior medics to never lose their passion for the craft of medicine. That way no matter where they are, no matter what they're doing, they can always be there for someone on their worst day.”

All American valor in action.

The U.S. military has always been fertile soil for firsts throughout our nation’s history, and the promotion of Carol A. Mutter to become the nation’s first female lieutenant general serves as a perfect case in point for Women’s History Month.

Women have served in the military from the earliest years of our representative republic.

Deborah Sampson (Gannett) served covertly when she disguised herself as a man under the assumed name of Robert Shurtleff, to join the Continental Army and fight in the Revolutionary War in 1782. Sampson went so far as to cut a musket ball out of her own thigh to prevent a battlefield surgeon from discovering her true gender. She was honorably discharged as a private in 1793.

Women gained the opportunity to serve openly in World War 1 when Congress opened the military to women in 1914. However, it took more than two centuries between the time Sampson first shouldered a musket to the time when women served as general (flag rank) officers in the American military. Mutter achieved one-star brigadier general rank in 1991.

Three years later Mutter became the first woman in the history of America’s military to achieve two-star major general rank in 1994, and two years after that in 1996 she became the first woman to become a three-star lieutenant general in any American military branch.

Born in 1945 in Greeley, Colorado, Mutter graduated in 1967 from officer candidate school at the University of Northern Colorado as a second lieutenant in the Marine Corps.

Mutter had a number of firsts during her 32-year career in the Corps:

•First woman to qualify as Command Center Crew Commander/Space Director at U.S. Space Command.
• First woman of flag rank (general officer rank) to command a major deployable tactical command.
• First woman Marine major general, and senior woman in all the services at that time.
• First woman nominated by a U.S. president (Bill Clinton) for three-star rank.
• First female lieutenant general in the U.S. Armed Forces.

During a 2014 interview for the documentary Unsung Heroes: The Story of America's Female Patriots, Mutter explains why she joined the Marine Corps during the early years of the Vietnam War.

“Because they're the best, there's no doubt about that,” she said. “ ... when I joined, (the Corps) was only one percent female and there were no women in the deployed forces at all. So, as long as the women were back in the rear doing the jobs that the men didn't want to do, there was not much of a problem.”

The general has been recognized as a trailblazer by several different organizations. Among them is the National Women’s Hall of Fame, which inducted the general in 2017.

Mutter retired from the Corps in 1999 and lives with her husband at their home in Lookout Mountain, Tennessee.

SSG Jamyn Peterson wouldn't describe himself as a hero, he said. However, during his last deployment to the remote Oruzgan province in Afghanistan from December 2006 until January 2008, the Army Reservist repeatedly demonstrated his dedication to his comrades and to his duties. Peterson was recognized for his service with a Purple Heart and two Bronze Star Medals, one with ‘Valor.'

The second Bronze Star recognized his performance as team leader as “absolutely phenomenal,” according to the award citation. But it was the bravery he demonstrated during an ambush that earned him the Bronze Star with ‘Valor.”

“I was honored,” Peterson said of receiving the medal, “but I was more honored that my guys got them.”

SSG Matt Winters and SGT Ben Mogenson were riding with him on June 16, 2007 when their convoy was ambushed on the road home. When a bomb exploded just feet from their truck, the truck leading the convoy sped ahead to avoid the blast. But they took a wrong turn.

Peterson and his team had a choice: stay on the road that led back to camp or follow their comrades the wrong way into enemy territory. They decided to follow their comrades.

It wasn't long before the first truck was hit by a rocket propelled grenade that went right through it, forcing everyone out of the truck. And while there were
only six soldiers between their two trucks, “there were over 100 bad guys. They were only 90 feet away. You could see them. They were just lined up,” he said.
“It was like hail coming down on the truck. It was like incessant bullets raining,” Peterson said. That's when he directed his vehicle right into the middle of the ambush to provide cover and support to the disabled vehicle.

“The one thing I remember was that I could have stayed in the truck and gotten killed, but if I got out of the truck I was going to get killed. Pretty much we were going to die,” he said. “Life flashes before you.”

But Peterson did get out of the truck, and was able to set up behind the hood of the disabled vehicle so he could provide cover while the other soldiers tended to the injured. They were able to hold the enemy at bay until Afghan Army soldiers arrived on the scene to help. When the enemy saw the two trucks with 15 Afghan soldiers in it, they started to flee, Peterson said.

“They kind of saved our lives,” Peterson said. “We'd built enough of a rapport,” he said, “that they came to help us.” It was an act which demonstrated not only their loyalty, but also their bravery, he said.

Peterson spoke as highly of Winters and Mogenson.

“They were more aware of what was going on. That's more brave than me,” he said. “Those guys were aware what was going on and still kept at it. They did a great job.”

Peterson, however, said he is most proud of his work with the people of the Oruzgan province. Working with the local community, he and his team set up the only local health clinic for miles around, a radio station, as well as a primary school for the local children that teaches reading, writing, arithmetic and Islam.

“Any good we wanted to do, we were able to do it,” Peterson said. “Being out in the middle of nowhere, I thought I was in a place where I belonged.”

Despite the enemy's opposition to the school, the students would get up at five in the morning to walk five miles to school. They would have to skirt Taliban checkpoints to avoid getting beaten, Peterson said.

“They are worried if they're going to get beaten with sticks on the way to school, and they'd still come,” Peterson said. The enemy “rocketed us twice while the students were in there, but they kept coming.”

“It was a pretty amazing experience. A good learning experience,” he said of the deployment. “That's one thing that I take away from this, how the human being can adapt to any situation.”

Peterson is still an active reservist training troops heading to Afghanistan.

“That's what I have a passion for now, making sure that these troops are ready to hit the ground when they go down range,” he said.

Peterson, who will likely redeploy shortly, said it's important to remember that the army is made up of individual men and women.

“If I don't go, someone less experienced will have to go. There's an obligation there,” he said. “Somebody's got to do it.”

MARINE CORPS AIR GROUND COMBAT CENTER TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. --

Famous French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte once said, “Valor is a gift. Those having it never know for sure whether they have it till the test comes.”
In a ceremony at Lance Cpl. Torrey L. Gray Field Thursday, a Marine who was tested in the heat of battle received the highest award for valor given by the Department of the Navy, the Navy Cross Medal, and was meritoriously promoted to the rank of corporal.

Cpl. Richard S. Weinmaster, a Squad Automatic Weapon gunner with 3rd Platoon, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, received the award for his actions as a private first class in Afghanistan’s Helmand Province on July 8, 2008 in support of Operation Enduring Freedom.

According to his platoon commander, 1st Lt. George Fenton, Weinmaster, a Cozad, Neb., native, was in front of a squad-sized patrol making its way through an eight-foot wide alley bordered on each side by 10-foot tall mud-brick walls, dubbed “ambush alley,” when their patrol was attacked by enemy small-arms fire and grenades.

In the midst of the firefight, Weinmaster provided accurate suppressive fire with his SAW until he noticed an incoming grenade land near his team leader, Lance Cpl. Tyler Wilkerson.

Fenton, a Fredericksburg, Va., native, explained how Weinmaster shoved Wilkerson out of the way then jumped toward the grenade to try and smother the blast. As he jumped, the grenade exploded sending the majority of its shrapnel into Weinmaster.

Weinmaster effectively shielded his team leader from the blast and Wilkerson was spared from any shrapnel. Weinmaster, however, received serious wounds, including a piece of shrapnel that entered his left eye socket and traveled halfway into his brain, where it remains to this day.

Despite his grave injuries, Weinmaster re-mounted his SAW and continued to provide effective suppressive fire on the enemy positions 50 yards away.

Staff Sgt. Kyle Lockhart, Weinmaster’s former platoon sergeant, said Weinmaster’s heroic actions in the heat of battle are a true reflection of his caliber.

Lockhart said for a Marine two-and-a-half months into his first deployment who has been in the Marine Corps for just a year to show such heroism is proof real valor and selflessness remain in the heart of Marines everywhere.

“Valor has to come from the heart and soul,” said Jim Weinmaster, Cpl. Weinmaster’s father. “It has to come from within. Karen [Weinmaster’s mother] and I raised him as best as we could, but actions like that go beyond parenting, beyond anything that can be taught.”

Weinmaster remained humble throughout the ceremony as well as afterward when he was greeted and thanked by scores of Marines, former Marines and grateful civilians.

“I didn’t do anything special,” he told everyone. “Everyone on my left and right would have done the same thing. I was just in the right place at the right time.”

Fenton and Lockhart agreed, saying that their platoon was full of Marines who would have done the same if given the opportunity, but both also emphasized the fact Weinmaster was given the opportunity and he acted in total disregard for his own safety to save another Marine’s life.

His devotion and selflessness earned Weinmaster the Navy Cross, although he maintains he was “just doing his job.”
